stories.headline: Cyclone batters Krishna district
stories.title: Cyclone batters Krishna district
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Machilipatnam: Cyclone Arnab’s impact triggered heavy rainfall accompanied by strong winds across Krishna district on Wednesday, inundating roads, uprooting trees and hoardings, and disrupting normal life in several coastal mandals.
Koduru recorded the highest rainfall in the district at 165.8 mm, according to the mandal-wise rainfall report.
The district received an average rainfall of 68.7 mm, with a cumulative total of 1,787.4 mm.

Coastal mandals bore the brunt of the downpour, with Machilipatnam North and Machilipatnam South each recording 112.6 mm, followed by Nagayalanka at 108.8 mm, Pedana at 103.2 mm and Guduru at 102.2 mm.
Avanigadda recorded 97.4 mm, Challapalli 88.4 mm, Pamarru 68.6 mm and Ghantasala 68.2 mm.
Bapulapadu registered the lowest rainfall at 26.2 mm.

The situation was particularly alarming in Venugopalapuram village of Koduru mandal in the Avanigadda constituency, where incessant rain since Tuesday night and powerful winds left roads waterlogged and brought down large trees across roads.
Villagers expressed fears of a situation similar to the devastating 1977 cyclone.
Their concerns were compounded by difficulties in accessing routes out of the village.
A bridge near Lingannakodu on the Ullipalem side was reportedly damaged, while the road towards Salempalem was unavailable, leaving residents facing serious connectivity problems.

stories.title: Cyclone Arnab disrupts life in Krishna, NTR districts
stories.summary: Cyclone Arnab disrupts life in Krishna, NTR districts
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Vijayawada: Cyclone Arnab battered Krishna and NTR districts with heavy rain and strong winds on Wednesday, inundating low-lying areas, damaging standing crops, uprooting trees and disrupting normal life.
Machilipatnam and Vijayawada witnessed widespread waterlogging, while power outages left several localities without electricity.
According to preliminary Agriculture Department reports, crops were inundated across 35,789 hectares in the two districts, with paddy accounting for the bulk of the affected area.
Krishna district recorded an average rainfall of 68.7 mm, according to district figures.
Coastal mandals bore the brunt of the downpour, with Machilipatnam North and South recording 112.6 mm each, followed by Nagayalanka (108.8 mm), Pedana (103.2 mm) and Guduru (102.2 mm).
Avanigadda received 97.4 mm, Challapalli 88.4 mm, Pamarru 68.6 mm and Ghantasala 68.2 mm, while Bapulapadu recorded 26.2 mm.
In Venugopalapuram village of Koduru mandal in Avanigadda constituency, incessant rain and strong winds since Tuesday night inundated roads and uprooted large trees, obstructing traffic.
In Machilipatnam, rainwater flooded several roads and the RTC bus stand, while fallen trees further disrupted traffic and daily activities.
According to the Agriculture Department’s preliminary report, crops were affected across 35,273 hectares in Krishna district.
Paddy accounted for 34,864 hectares, followed by blackgram (358 hectares), sugarcane (25 hectares), groundnut (23 hectares) and sesamum (three hectares).
Minister Kollu Ravindra visited affected areas in Krishna district and alerted officials to take immediate measures to clear waterlogging and restore normalcy.
In NTR district, Vijayawada city experienced widespread waterlogging, with knee-deep rainwater accumulating on several roads.

stories.title: Cyclone Arnab: Control room activated in Bhadrachalam, preparedness reviewed
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Several areas in Bhadradri Kothagudem and Khammam districts witnessed intermittent drizzle on Wednesday under the influence of Cyclone Arnab.
A control room was set up at the Bhadrachalam sub-Collector’s office to respond to emergencies, which can be reached at 08743-232444.
Schools, colleges and Anganwadi centres in Bhadradri Kothagudem district remained closed as a precautionary measure.

Bhadrachalam Sub-Collector Mrinal Shreshtha reviewed cyclone preparedness with officials from the police, National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), District Disaster Response Force (DDRF), and Fire Services Department on preparedness to ensure coordinated response measures.
He also visited vulnerable areas in the temple town to assess the situation.

article_sentences: Rajamahendravaram: East Godavari joint collector Y Megha Swaroop and Rajamahendravaram Sub-Collector Shubham Nokhwal visited Kapileswarapuram mandal on Wednesday and reviewed the situation in the wake of heavy rains and flooding caused by Cyclone Arnab.
The officials held a meeting with the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) team deployed in the mandal at the Tahsildar’s office.
They enquired about the flood situation, relief measures being taken in inundated areas and precautionary steps being implemented to protect residents.
The joint collector and sub-collector directed the NDRF personnel to remain alert and respond immediately to any emergency.
District Fire Officer Martin Luther King also attended the meeting.

He writes extensively on politics, tribal affairs, rural development, tourism, development, and human-interest stories.

stories.headline: Bihar MLC polls: Upper caste candidates dominate election results
stories.title: Bihar MLC polls: Upper caste candidates dominate election results
stories.summary: The Opposition Congress party which had put up its candidates on five seats has failed to win even a single seat in the elections
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'election results' in title weight 64
article_sentences: Out of eight State legislative Council seats which had gone to poll on October 23, 2026 and final results of them which were scheduled to be announced on October 27, some are new faces with upper caste dominating the poll on six seats while, the Backward caste and Extremely backward caste candidates won one seat each respectively from Kosi and Tirhut Graduate constituencies.

Out of eight seats, the upper-caste Bhumihar candidates won on five seats and one by a Rajput candidate while, the Other Backward (Yadav) and Extremely Backward Caste (mallah---boatmen/ Fishermen) candidates won on one seat each from Kosi and Tirhut Graduate constituencies.
The Opposition Congress party which had put up its candidates on five seats has failed to win even a single seat in the elections.

Five upper-caste Bhumihar candidates are Neeraj Kumar Singh (Patna Graduate), Sanjiv Kumar Singh (Patna Teachers), Suresh Rai (Darbhanga Teachers), Sarvesh Kumar (Darbhanga Graduate) and Narendra Singh (Tirhut Teachers).

Out of these five upper caste winning candidates, three Sarvesh Kumar (Darbhanga Graduate seat) and Narendra Singh (Tirhut Teachers seat), and from the other ruling coalition partner JD-U is Neeraj Kumar Singh from Patna Graduate seat are from ruling NDA bloc while, the other two from upper caste Bhumihar community are: Opposition Rashtriya Janata Dal Sanjiv Kumar from Patna Teachers seat and Jan Suraaj Party candidate Suresh Rai from Darbhanga Teachers seats.

One Independent candidate Rahul Raj from Saran Teachers constituency is from upper caste Rajput community while, Narendra Kumar Yadav from BJP from Kosi Graduate seat is from Other Backward Yadav (OBC) caste and the Extremely Backward Caste (EBC) candidate Vanshidhar Brajwasi is from mallah (boatman, Fishermen) community who won the poll from Tirhut Graduate seat as an Independent candidate.

Out of eight, the new faces are Sanjiv Kumar Singh from RJD, who won the Patna Teachers constituency, defeating the several-time MLC from the seat, Nawal Kishore Yadav from BJP, Suresh Rai from Jan Suraaj Party, who won from Darbhanga Teachers seat, defeating the veteran sitting Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha, Rahul Raj, the Independent candidate from Saran Teachers constituency and the Tirhut Graduate constituency candidate Vanshidhar Brajwasi.

stories.headline: Ashok accuses State Election Commission of printing 90 lakh voter cards after announcement of SIR; SEC denies charge
stories.title: Ashok accuses State Election Commission of printing 90 lakh voter cards after announcement of SIR; SEC denies charge
stories.summary: Leader of Opposition in the Assembly R. Ashok has accused the State Election Commission of violating norms to facilitate irregularities in the proposed GBA polls by printing 90 lakh voters’ identity cards in Bengaluru at a cost of ₹20 crore after the announcement of Special Intensive Revision by the Election Commission of India
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Leader of Opposition in the Assembly R. Ashok has accused the State Election Commission (SEC) of violating norms to facilitate irregularities in the proposed GBA polls by printing 90 lakh voters’ identity cards in Bengaluru at a cost of ₹20 crore after the announcement of Special Intensive Revision (SIR) by the Election Commission of India.
Alleging that the Congress government was involved in these irregularities, Mr. Ashok demanded a CBI probe into the episode.
However, the SEC strongly denied these allegations by stating that the tenders had been floated before the announcement of SIR and that it had acted within its legal mandate.
Addressing a press conference in Bengaluru, Mr. Ashok alleged that the SEC had printed 90 lakh cards, though the total number of voters in Bengaluru had been pegged at around 59 lakh after the SIR.
Pointing out that the SEC was now left with an additional 31 lakh voters identity cards, he described these additional cards as “bogus” and alleged that they would be used for “vote theft”.
He alleged that the Congress government had got this done to commit irregularities in the proposed election to GBA.

“The State Election Commission did this though it had filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court stating that elections to local bodies would be held only after the SIR and after the new voters’ list is prepared,“ he said.
Denying the allegations, SEC Secretary Amaresh H. said the tender was called before the SIR was announced.
Mr. Amaresh said the tender was issued under Rule 26 of the Greater Bengaluru Governance (Registration of Electors) Rules, 2025, which provides for the printing of voter identity cards.
He said the SEC had acted within its legal mandate and that the SIR did not require it to suspend its work relating to local body electoral processes.
“The SIR is not binding on the State Election Commission in the manner being suggested.
Local body elections and elections conducted by the Election Commission of India are governed by different frameworks,” he said.

stories.headline: Cooperative Federalism: The Constitutional Compact India Must Renew
stories.title: Cooperative Federalism: The Constitutional Compact India Must Renew
stories.summary: India’s federalism is not a contest over who commands and who complies. It is a constitutional compact designed to reconcile national unity with regional autonomy, common purpose with political diversity, and effective governance with democratic accountability. Its success depends not on the concentration of power in one centre, but on the capacity of the Union and the States to exercise their respective constitutional responsibilities in partnership. As India confronts increasingly complex economic, environmental, technological and geopolitical challenges, cooperative federalism has become more than a constitutional aspiration. It is an essential condition of democratic stability, institutional trust and effective government. The constitutional scholar Granville Austin captured this distinctive design in The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation, describing India’s model as one of “cooperative federalism.” His insight remains relevant: India’s federal structure was shaped by the need to preserve national unity while accommodating an extraordinary diversity of languages, cultures, political traditions and regional aspirations. The constitutional challenge was never simply to distribute power, but to make that distribution work. The constitutional architecture of cooperation The Constitution does not expressly use the phrase “cooperative federalism,” but its institutional architecture reflects that philosophy. Article 1 describes India as a “Union of States.” Articles 245 and 246, read with the Seventh Schedule, distribute legislative powers between the Union and the States. Articles 256 and 257 address aspects of executive coordination, while Articles 268 to 293 govern financial relations. Article 263 provides for an Inter-State Council, and Article 280 establishes the Finance Commission. These provisions establish both the autonomy of constitutional authorities and the need for coordination. They do not envisage government as a collection of watertight compartments. The Constitution also gives the Union significant powers, reflecting the historical circumstances of Partition and the imperative of national integration. Yet this central strength must not be confused with an unrestricted authority to displace State autonomy. The constitutional framework requires a balance between national interests and the legitimate responsibilities of elected State governments. The Supreme Court’s decision in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) reinforced the constitutional significance of federalism, while the Court’s wider jurisprudence has emphasised that constitutional powers must be exercised within their prescribed limits. Federalism is therefore not merely an administrative arrangement. It is part of the constitutional structure through which democracy is organised, and power is held accountable. A strong Union requires strong States The false choice between a strong Union and strong States must be rejected. National unity is not weakened when States exercise legitimate autonomy; it is strengthened when regional aspirations find democratic expression within the constitutional framework. India’s federal experiment differs from federations formed through an agreement among previously sovereign political units. Its Constitution sought to preserve the unity of an exceptionally diverse country while assigning substantial responsibilities to different levels of government. That design requires flexibility, consultation and mutual respect. States are not administrative branches of the Union. They possess constitutionally defined powers and independent democratic mandates. Equally, State autonomy does not extinguish the Union’s responsibility for national security, macroeconomic stability and matters constitutionally entrusted to it. The objective must be constitutional partnership, not institutional rivalry. Political diversity must not become federal discrimination India’s democratic landscape is marked by different political parties governing at the Centre and across the States. This is neither an anomaly nor a constitutional inconvenience. It is a natural expression of electoral pluralism. The Constitution recognises governments formed through democratic processes, not governments entitled to cooperation only when their political affiliations coincide. A State government cannot be treated as an adversary merely because it belongs to the Opposition. Nor should legitimate access to national resources, institutional consultation or development opportunities depend on political alignment. The true test of cooperative federalism arises when governments disagree. Constitutional maturity lies in managing differences through dialogue, established institutions and law—not through confrontation, public recrimination or the politicisation of constitutional offices. Governments change; the federal compact must endure. Fiscal federalism: Autonomy requires resources The most consequential test of federalism is financial. States deliver many of the public services citizens experience directly, including healthcare, education, policing, agriculture, welfare and local infrastructure. Yet their ability to discharge these responsibilities depends substantially on the distribution of taxation powers, transfers and grants. A federation cannot function equitably if responsibilities are decentralised while financial discretion is disproportionately centralised. The Finance Commission is therefore a pivotal constitutional institution. Tax devolution and grants-in-aid must be guided by transparent principles that reconcile the needs of less-developed States, population-related responsibilities, fiscal discipline and developmental performance. States also require sufficient fiscal space to respond to local priorities and innovate in public policy. Predictable transfers, timely payments and meaningful consultation are essential to that autonomy. Fiscal federalism should not become a relationship between a permanent donor and a dependent recipient. It must recognise the States as partners in generating national prosperity and delivering constitutional promises. The GST Council: Cooperation without compulsory unanimity The Goods and Services Tax Council, established under Article 279A, offers an important institutional example. It brings the Union and the States into a common forum to deliberate on significant questions of indirect taxation and the functioning of the GST system. The experience has also exposed tensions over revenue compensation, fiscal autonomy, tax rates and the balance between uniformity and State flexibility. These disagreements do not necessarily indicate failure. Federal systems are designed to accommodate competing interests. The real test is whether institutional mechanisms permit disagreements to be negotiated fairly. The GST Council’s enduring lesson is that cooperation does not require unanimity on every question. It requires a genuine commitment to consultation, reasoned compromise and shared responsibility. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how closely national coordination and State-level implementation are connected. It also exposed the costs of inadequate consultation and uneven institutional capacity. The lesson extends to future public health emergencies, environmental crises and technological disruptions. Renewing the institutions of federal dialogue India already possesses institutions capable of strengthening this partnership, but their effectiveness depends on regular engagement and political will. The Inter-State Council under Article 263 should be used more consistently for structured discussion of Centre-State relations and inter-State disputes. The GST Council should remain a forum for meaningful negotiation, and NITI Aayog should facilitate substantive policy cooperation rather than merely communicate decisions already taken. Parliament, too, must give serious consideration to State perspectives when legislative proposals substantially affect their constitutional responsibilities. Consultation must occur early enough to influence policy. It cannot be reduced to a procedural formality after decisions have effectively been made. Constitutional morality and the road ahead Ultimately, cooperative federalism depends as much on constitutional morality as on institutional design. The Union must respect legitimate State autonomy; States must recognise legitimate national interests; Governors must act impartially; and elected governments must exercise their powers responsibly. Political parties must distinguish the interests of the Republic from the immediate advantages of partisan competition. The gravest threat to federalism is not disagreement. It is the erosion of institutional trust through the politicisation of constitutional powers. India’s federal compact must now be renewed through transparent fiscal arrangements, predictable intergovernmental cooperation, stronger consultation and scrupulous respect for constitutional boundaries. The question is not whether the Union or the States should prevail. It is whether both can discharge their responsibilities more effectively by working together. A confident India must be a confident Union of confident States. As Granville Austin’s understanding of cooperative federalism reminds us, national unity and regional autonomy need not be competing objectives. Properly balanced, they reinforce each other. Cooperative federalism is not a concession from the Union to the States. It is a constitutional obligation arising from the structure of the Republic. Renewing that compact is essential to India’s democratic credibility, developmental ambitions and constitutional future. opening: India’s federalism is not a contest over who commands and who complies.
It is a constitutional compact designed to reconcile national unity with regional autonomy, common purpose with political diversity, and effective governance with democratic accountability.

As India confronts increasingly complex economic, environmental, technological and geopolitical challenges, cooperative federalism has become more than a constitutional aspiration.
It is an essential condition of democratic stability, institutional trust and effective government.

The constitutional scholar Granville Austin captured this distinctive design in The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation, describing India’s model as one of “cooperative federalism.” His insight remains relevant: India’s federal structure was shaped by the need to preserve national unity while accommodating an extraordinary diversity of languages, cultures, political traditions and regional aspirations.
The constitutional challenge was never simply to distribute power, but to make that distribution work.
The constitutional architecture of cooperation.
The Constitution does not expressly use the phrase “cooperative federalism,” but its institutional architecture reflects that philosophy.
Article 1 describes India as a “Union of States.” Articles 245 and 246, read with the Seventh Schedule, distribute legislative powers between the Union and the States.
Articles 256 and 257 address aspects of executive coordination, while Articles 268 to 293 govern financial relations.
Article 263 provides for an Inter-State Council, and Article 280 establishes the Finance Commission.
These provisions establish both the autonomy of constitutional authorities and the need for coordination.
They do not envisage government as a collection of watertight compartments.
The Constitution also gives the Union significant powers, reflecting the historical circumstances of Partition and the imperative of national integration.
Yet this central strength must not be confused with an unrestricted authority to displace State autonomy.
The constitutional framework requires a balance between national interests and the legitimate responsibilities of elected State governments.
The Supreme Court’s decision in S.R. Bommai.

Union of India (1994) reinforced the constitutional significance of federalism, while the Court’s wider jurisprudence has emphasised that constitutional powers must be exercised within their prescribed limits.
Federalism is therefore not merely an administrative arrangement.
It is part of the constitutional structure through which democracy is organised, and power is held accountable.
A strong Union requires strong States.
The false choice between a strong Union and strong States must be rejected.
National unity is not weakened when States exercise legitimate autonomy; it is strengthened when regional aspirations find democratic expression within the constitutional framework.
India’s federal experiment differs from federations formed through an agreement among previously sovereign political units.
Its Constitution sought to preserve the unity of an exceptionally diverse country while assigning substantial responsibilities to different levels of government.
That design requires flexibility, consultation and mutual respect.
States are not administrative branches of the Union.
They possess constitutionally defined powers and independent democratic mandates.
Equally, State autonomy does not extinguish the Union’s responsibility for national security, macroeconomic stability and matters constitutionally entrusted to it.
The objective must be constitutional partnership, not institutional rivalry.
Political diversity must not become federal discrimination India’s democratic landscape is marked by different political parties governing at the Centre and across the States.
This is neither an anomaly nor a constitutional inconvenience.
It is a natural expression of electoral pluralism.
The Constitution recognises governments formed through democratic processes, not governments entitled to cooperation only when their political affiliations coincide.
A State government cannot be treated as an adversary merely because it belongs to the Opposition.
Nor should legitimate access to national resources, institutional consultation or development opportunities depend on political alignment.
The true test of cooperative federalism arises when governments disagree.

Constitutional maturity lies in managing differences through dialogue, established institutions and law—not through confrontation, public recrimination or the politicisation of constitutional offices.
Governments change; the federal compact must endure.

States deliver many of the public services citizens experience directly, including healthcare, education, policing, agriculture, welfare and local infrastructure.

A federation cannot function equitably if responsibilities are decentralised while financial discretion is disproportionately centralised.
The Finance Commission is therefore a pivotal constitutional institution.

States also require sufficient fiscal space to respond to local priorities and innovate in public policy.
Predictable transfers, timely payments and meaningful consultation are essential to that autonomy.
Fiscal federalism should not become a relationship between a permanent donor and a dependent recipient.
It must recognise the States as partners in generating national prosperity and delivering constitutional promises.

article_sentences: Billionaire Gautam Adani, India’s richest person, is exploring a potential acquisition of Dutch energy storage group VTTI as supply disruptions make the facilities more valuable for energy trading, people familiar with the matter said.
Adani Group, the tycoon’s power-to-ports conglomerate, is among suitors that have been evaluating Rotterdam-based VTTI, according to the people.
A deal could value the company at around €3 billion ($3.4 billion), they said.
Australian infrastructure manager IFM Investors Pty and energy and commodities group Vitol SA each own around 45% of VTTI, while Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.
holds the remaining 10%.

Adnoc is considering selling out of VTTI completely and the other co-owners may also look to reduce their positions in the company in any deal, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing confidential information.
Deliberations are ongoing and there’s no certainty they’ll result in a transaction, the people said.
Other bidders have also been pursuing a stake in VTTI, they said.
A representative for Adani Group didn’t immediately respond to queries.
Spokespeople for IFM, Adnoc and VTTI declined to comment.
A representative for Vitol didn’t immediately comment.
VTTI operates terminals used to store fuels and chemicals, including fossil fuels, biofuels and solvents.

article_sentences: The Allahabad High Court Bar Association has approached the Chief Justice over a lawyer's alleged humiliation in court.
The dispute has triggered boycott discussions amid concerns about advocates' dignity.

The Allahabad High Court Bar Association has threatened to boycott the court of Justice Ajay Bhanot over the alleged humiliation of a lawyer during proceedings in Court No. 49, accusing the judge of undermining the dignity of the legal fraternity.

In a letter dated October 27 to the Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court, the association demanded appropriate action and warned that it would boycott the judge’s court if the matter was not addressed.

The letter, signed by Bar Association president Dr CP Upadhyay and general secretary Santosh Kumar Mishra, detailed an incident involving a district Superintendent of Police (SP), an Additional Government Advocate (AGA) and a lawyer.
According to the letter, Justice Bhanot had directed that a separate chair be placed in the row behind the lawyers for police officers or other senior officials appearing in his courtroom.
During proceedings on Tuesday, an SP-rank officer was seated behind the AGA when a lawyer politely asked him to move to the designated seat, saying it was not his place.
The AGA allegedly rebuked the lawyer and threatened to complain to the judge when he arrived.
After Justice Bhanot entered the courtroom, the AGA raised the issue with him.
The association alleged that the judge pointed a finger at the lawyer, used harsh language and ordered that he be sent to jail.
When the lawyer asked the police officer to forgive him, the judge allegedly insisted that he apologise to the SP.
The lawyer subsequently apologised to the officer, the letter claimed.
